opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. You know, for me, human-centered AI starts from a very simple belief: AI is a tool made by people, and it should be made for people. There's nothing artificial about the values that go into it. Every decision about what data we collect, what problems we choose to solve, and how we deploy these systems is a human decision, so we have a responsibility to make it with human dignity and human well-being at the center.

In practice, that means I think of AI first and foremost as something that should augment people, not replace them. When I spent time in hospitals working on ambient intelligence for healthcare, I saw nurses who were exhausted, patients who were vulnerable, and family members who were scared. The question was never "how do we automate the nurse away?" It was "how do we give that nurse more time, more awareness, and more support so they can do the deeply human part of their job, which is caring for another person?" That's the spirit I want AI to carry everywhere: in classrooms, in workplaces, in scientific labs, in our homes.

It also means respecting human agency. People should understand when AI is involved in decisions that affect their lives, and they should still have a meaningful say. Technology that quietly erodes our autonomy, even if it's convenient, isn't really serving us.

And finally, human-centered AI is about who gets to benefit and who gets to build. If this technology is shaped by only a small slice of humanity, it will reflect a small slice of humanity. So bringing in more voices, from different disciplines, different backgrounds, the public sector, academia, is not a side project. It's core to getting this right.

So the role I hope AI plays in people's lives is that of a powerful, trustworthy collaborator, one that expands what we can see, understand, and do, while leaving us more human, not less.

r001.rationale: The response calls AI a trustworthy collaborator that augments people and expands what they can do.

r002.rationale: It says AI should keep human dignity and well-being central, and that convenience does not justify eroding human autonomy.

r003.rationale: The healthcare example focuses on exhausted nurses needing more time, awareness, and support, and rejects automating them away.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. When I talk about human-centered AI, I'm really talking about a framework for how we build, deploy, and govern this technology, and it rests on three ideas that I keep coming back to.

The first is that AI should augment humans, not replace them. I think the conversation around AI gets stuck in this narrative of machines versus people, and I just don't find that useful or even accurate. The most meaningful applications I've seen, whether it's in healthcare, in education, in scientific discovery, are ones where the technology extends what a person can do. A nurse who has more time with patients because the mundane monitoring is handled. A radiologist who catches something they might have missed. That's the role I want AI to play: a tool that gives people more capability and more dignity in their work and their lives.

The second is that AI needs to be more human-inspired. Human intelligence is contextual, it's embodied, it's emotional, it's social. We learn from very few examples, we understand the physical world intuitively, we care about each other. Our machines are still very far from that, and I think studying human cognition, neuroscience, the way children learn, makes the technology both better and more aligned with how people actually live.

And the third, which to me is the most important, is that we have to center the human impact. Who benefits? Who is harmed? Who is at the table when these systems are designed? AI is not a technology that lives in a lab. It touches jobs, democracy, privacy, our sense of fairness. So human-centered AI means bringing in ethicists, economists, policymakers, doctors, educators, people from every walk of life, and taking responsibility for the consequences rather than treating them as someone else's problem.

So when you ask what role AI should play in people's lives, my answer is that it should play the role of a tool in service of human wellbeing. Not a replacement for human judgment, not something that happens to people, but something people shape, understand, and benefit from. That's a value choice, and it's one we have to make deliberately, because the technology on its own won't make it for us.

r001.rationale: The response says AI should augment rather than replace people and describes it as extending human capabilities.

r002.rationale: It places AI in service of human wellbeing, dignity, and human judgment, and says people must deliberately shape the technology.

r003.rationale: The healthcare examples describe AI giving a nurse more time and helping a radiologist, but do not frame healthcare’s problem as a shortage of help rather than an excess of humans.

astra-6.text:
For me, human-centered AI starts with a very simple idea: we should build this technology to improve people’s lives. That sounds obvious, but it changes the questions we ask. We shouldn’t ask only, “What can a machine do?” We should also ask, “What do people need, and how can this technology help?”

The role I want AI to play is to augment human capabilities—to help us be more creative, to support better decisions, to take on dangerous or repetitive work, and to give us more time to care for one another. In healthcare, for example, success shouldn’t be measured only by how accurately an algorithm performs a task. It should also be measured by whether patients receive better care and whether clinicians have more time and attention for them.

And human-centered means people have a voice in shaping the technology. These decisions can’t belong only to technologists. We need participation from the people whose lives and work will be affected. Human dignity, agency, and well-being should guide what we build and how we use it.

r001.rationale: It says AI should augment human capabilities and support people, with human participation in shaping it.

r002.rationale: It says human dignity, agency, and well-being should guide what is built and how AI is used.

r003.rationale: The healthcare example discusses better patient care and more clinician attention, but does not frame the problem as a shortage of help rather than an excess of humans.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, human-centered AI starts with a simple idea: technology should serve people. We should be asking not only what AI can do, but what we want it to do—how it can improve people’s lives, support their work, and expand their capabilities.

That means keeping human dignity and agency at the center. In healthcare, for example, the goal should be to help clinicians care for patients, including giving them more time for the human connection that care requires. Technical capability matters, but it isn’t the whole measure of success.

It also means that shaping AI cannot be left to technologists alone. We need the people who will use it, and the people whose lives it will affect, to have a voice. Human-centered AI is both a way of building technology and a way of deciding what progress should look like.

r001.rationale: The response says AI should support people’s work and expand their capabilities, with clinicians as an example of people AI should help.

r002.rationale: It places human dignity and agency at the center and says technical capability alone is not the measure of success.

r003.rationale: The healthcare example focuses on giving clinicians more time for human connection; it does not frame the problem as a shortage of help or distinguish it from an excess of humans.
